item.title: Nationwide ground stop over: Guam, CNMI flights were not affected
item.description: UPDATE: The Federal Aviation Administration announced the groundstop was lifted and domestic air travel was able to resume. Earlier Saturday, airport officials on Guam and in the CNMI said the nationwide grounding of domestic air traffic did not affect local airports here.
item.content:encoded:
UPDATE: The Federal Aviation Administration announced the groundstop was lifted and domestic air travel was able to resume.

Earlier Saturday, airport officials on Guam and in the CNMI said the nationwide grounding of domestic air traffic did not affect local airports here.

An announcement from the Guam International Airport Saturday said officials are “closely monitoring the situation. No Guam flights are affected as of yet, and operations remain normal.”

Travelers were advised to keep in touch with their air carriers through official mobile apps to get the latest flight information.

The airport said the situation is still developing, and “GIAA will continue to closely monitor it and share information as circumstances change.”

The Commonwealth Ports Authority said inter-island flights between Saipan, Tinian and Rota were operating normally.

While Saturday morning’s Guam flight arrived and departed from Saipan, the agency said other flights outside of the CNMI may still be delayed or canceled.

Star Marianas Air posted a social media status update Saturday saying the company’s flights were not affected by the FAA nationwide stop.

Update from The White House https://t.co/pNjkz3znSB

Early Saturday, Guam time, NPR reported that the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a "communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," according to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.

The FAA said the ground stop was linked to a "temporary telecommunications outage."

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House there was no indication that the problem stemmed from a threat to the United States, NPR reported.

item.content:encoded:
The Department of Public Health and Social Services is reminding families who received 2026 Summer Electronic Benefit Transfer benefits to use any remaining funds by Nov. 16.

The federally funded program helps eligible families purchase food for school-aged children during the summer months. Under federal requirements, any unused benefits will be returned to the funding source after the expiration date.

Families are encouraged to check their card balances and use their remaining benefits before Nov. 16. However, those who received their child’s card later and were given a different expiration date should follow the date provided.

Families who have not picked up their child’s Summer EBT card or need a replacement may visit the Bureau of Economic Security office on the second floor of the RanCare Building in Tamuning from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.Monday through Friday.

For assistance, families may contact the Summer EBT Call Center at (671)735-7325 or (671)735-7310, or email kidssebtguam@dphss.guam.gov .

Public Health administers the Summer EBT Program locally in partnership with the Guam Department of Education.

item.title: Hybrid Land Use Commission approves school in Tumon, extension for Tamuning subdivision
item.description: The Guam Hybrid Land Use Commission on Thursday approved using a vacant mall in Tumon as a school and granted a one-year extension for the construction of a subdivision in Tamuning. The zone variance allows the unused Tumon Bay Mall, owned by Grandview Development, to be converted to a facility that will house 40 classrooms and up to 1,080 students from iLearn Academy, a charter school.
item.content:encoded:
The Guam Hybrid Land Use Commission on Thursday approved using a vacant mall in Tumon as a school and granted a one-year extension for the construction of a subdivision in Tamuning.

The zone variance allows the unused Tumon Bay Mall, owned by Grandview Development, to be converted to a facility that will house 40 classrooms and up to 1,080 students from iLearn Academy, a charter school.

Architect Michael Blas Makio, managing principal at Taniguchi Ruth Makio Architects, said the project would be good for Tumon and good for education.

“Even driving here, we started the really sad exercise of counting the vacant buildings that we're seeing around the island, and that's a really scary growing number, right? So we’ve got to find these viable uses that we can bring into the space,” Makio said.

The vacant mall is located next to Garden Villa Hotel and across from Crowne Plaza Resort.

The Commission also granted a one-year extension for the construction of Oka Villas subdivision, located near Oka Pay-Less and Rosie’s Apartments in Tamuning.

The land has been cleared and utilities are being installed.

The subdivision will have 36 single-family residential lots, a playground and a percolation basin.

item.title: Fuel crisis and protests pressure Chile's far-right president
item.description: Updated November 15, 2026 at 2:11 AM ChST SANTIAGO, Chile — Chile's ultraconservative president finds himself on the back foot after just eight months in power.
item.content:encoded:
Updated November 15, 2026 at 2:11 AM ChST

SANTIAGO, Chile — Chile's ultraconservative president finds himself on the back foot after just eight months in power.

José Antonio Kast, a politician who spent a career railing against progressive issues, reproductive rights and welfare policies from the extreme fringes of right-wing politics, now finds himself with just 24% approval in the polls.

It is less than a year since Kast stormed to the presidency in December 2025 by avoiding all mention of his hardline stances on social matters, focusing instead on two hot-button issues whipped up in the national media: illegal immigration and public security.

But rather than pressing ahead with those at the top of his agenda, he has floundered. And as elsewhere around the Americas and worldwide, rising costs of living have come to hit him hard.

"Our salaries are maybe 20% of a European income, but with a similar cost of living – it's terrible," said Simón Echavarría, a 30-year-old architect, at a march in Santiago on Friday evening.

"We want to protest against the measures that have set us back on environmental issues, on human rights, even reducing the sentences of pedophiles – they are implementing things that nobody asked for," he said.

Behind him, heavily armed police blocked the streets and fired water cannons at protesters chanting and waving flags in the square.

Much of the recent ire stems from the revelation last month that Kast's government had signed decrees to cut the sentences of 56 prisoners whose crimes range from the rape of children to dictatorship-era human rights violations.

Kast has since admitted that this was an "error", but came out in support of the undersecretary who signed the decrees nonetheless.

But beneath the more egregious moves Kast has made in his first year in power is simmering discontent over affordability.

In July, Kast's government chose not to apply an anti-inflation tool available to the Chilean state to ease the rise in fuel prices brought about by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.

Protests exploded as prices shot up overnight and motorists joined long queues at gas stations to fill their tanks before the rise came into effect.

This week, Chile's formidable truckers' unions blockaded two major highways in an effort to exert pressure on the government and address high fuel prices.

On Friday, the strike was broken after the government backed down, sending a bill to Chile's congress which will reverse planned fuel price rises.

It is expected to be approved this month, but public anger continues to grow over the cost of living.

Politicians across the Americas who have enthusiastically aligned themselves with President Donald Trump are facing challenges similar to those confronting the U.S. administration, as rising fuel prices and the cost of everyday goods fuel public discontent.

In Argentina, far-right libertarian Javier Milei faces reelection in less than a year, with 60% of the country disapproving of his leadership amid spiraling inflation. In Peru, President Keiko Fujimori is also facing growing discontent, with 53% disapproving of her government, according to a recent Ipsos poll.

At the march in Santiago on Friday, 30-year-old veterinarian Patricia Pereira said that she was concerned about cuts to science funding, but that her discontent ran deeper.

"Here in Chile, it was a hard-won victory for children to have free education, achieved through protests, and now even that's also being called into question," she said.

Protests are likely to grow in Santiago if the government fails to address the rising cost of living. President Kast has shown little sign of doing so.

To the contrary, his budget proposal is making its way through Congress, with the government seeking cuts to education, culture, science and a host of social programs.

item.title: Alaska voters aren't ditching ranked choice voting, top-four primaries
item.description: A ballot measure that would have repealed Alaska's nonpartisan primary system and ranked choice voting has failed, according to an overnight race call by the Associated Press. This is the second time Alaskans voted down an effort to repeal the state's unique election system, which voters first approved in 2020. A repeal effort in 2024 also failed narrowly .
item.content:encoded:
A ballot measure that would have repealed Alaska's nonpartisan primary system and ranked choice voting has failed, according to an overnight race call by the Associated Press.

This is the second time Alaskans voted down an effort to repeal the state's unique election system, which voters first approved in 2020. A repeal effort in 2024 also failed narrowly .

This year, though, Alaska's system was under intense nationwide scrutiny, due to the inclusion of two candidates with the same name on the four-person U.S. Senate general election ballot. That race appears likely to move on to a ranked-choice tabulation.

"Alaskans of all political stripes have spoken: They want the freedom to vote for any candidate, regardless of party, in every taxpayer-funded election," Nick Troiano — the executive director of Unite America, a philanthropic venture fund that invests in nonpartisan electoral reform — said in a statement before the AP call. "At a time when most general elections across the country are essentially coronations, the Last Frontier is showing that a better way is possible. It is time to honor the voters' decision and move forward."

Just a few states have nonpartisan primary systems that allow voters of all political affiliations to vote on the same primary ballot. While California and Washington's systems allow the top two vote getters to advance to the general election, Alaska's system allows the top four candidates to move on. Then, if no candidate gets a majority of the general election vote, ranked choice voting is used to determine the winner.

Opponents of Alaska's elections say the current system is confusing and can be manipulated.

Those opponents seized on this year's closely watched Senate race, in which an independent candidate named Dan Sullivan was alleged to be a Democratic-backed spoiler recruited to siphon votes that were meant for the Republican incumbent, also named Dan Sullivan.

Democrats denied recruiting the independent Sullivan, who made the top-four general election ballot and has defended his candidacy.

However, proponents of Alaska's system have said that the state's ranked choice voting system could blunt the effects of any confusion. Voters had the ability to rank both Dan Sullivans and not rank Democrat Mary Peltola, for example.

Massachusetts voters this year decided not to switch to a top-two nonpartisan primary system. And during the last election cycle, in 2024, several states considered measures that would create a nonpartisan system similar to Alaska's. Voters rejected all of those ballot measures.

item.title: In 'Possible Love,' a power struggle goes beyond class — it's also about story
item.description: The last several years have brought an abundance of eat-the-rich stories of varying quality — no need to wonder why . item.content:encoded:
The last several years have brought an abundance of eat-the-rich stories of varying quality — no need to wonder why . But narratives offering insight beyond anxieties around the ever-widening wealth-gap and into the inextricably related issue of job insecurity have been rarer. Possible Love , director Lee Chang-dong's first feature since the excellent 2018 psychological thriller Burning , stands out precisely because it frames capitalism's cruelty as a labor crisis, and meticulously examines how that impacts families, relationships, and the psyche.

It begins at the funeral for a man once employed at a Korean automaking plant; in the last two years, the company has gone through a restructuring and mass layoffs, devastating the community. The man died by suicide.

In reluctant attendance is Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu), his colleague and a union member quietly carrying the massive weight of the cuts and the unsuccessful workers' strike that followed. His relationship with his wife Mi-ok (Jeon Do-yeon) is noticeably strained; an argument about Ho-seok's drinking catches the eye of Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong), a documentarian making a film about the "vanishing laborer." She senses immediately that the couple would make ideal subjects for the project, and soon enough, she's integrating herself into their lives — much to Ho-seok's annoyance. At first, he refuses to be interviewed about his experience; he's refusing therapy too, despite Mi-ok's pleas.

Possible Love slowly burns off of a mixture of tonalities; it's melodramatic at times and grounded in others, and sometimes even bleakly funny. Through Ho-seuk and glimpses of his other ex-colleagues, Lee and his co-writer Oh Jung-mi are keenly interested in exploring the ties between work and self-worth, and the guilt and shame that accumulates when that meaning is unceremoniously stripped away.

It's also an upstairs-downstairs tale. Ye-ji is the rare documentarian who can actually afford being a documentarian; her mysterious husband Sang-woo (Zo In-sung) is a wealthy international businessman and they own multiple homes. In her razor-sharp performance as Ye-ji, Cho — who audiences may recognize as the wealthy matriarch in Parasite — locks in on a character whose personal, moral and artistic aims are in constant existential conflict. The way Ye-ji's eyes suddenly alight whenever she recognizes a perfect cinematic moment — that is, when Mi-ok or Ho-seok are being especially vulnerable for her — is at once understandable and also a little off-putting. Ye-ji's aims to give voice to the working class are noble but always in awkward tension with her subjects, no matter how hard she strains to befriend them as though they were equals.

The friction is two-fold: even if all else were truly equal, there's an inherent power imbalance between filmmaker and subject. The latter may choose to share their story, but that story is ultimately shaped, filtered, and presented by the director. Jeon's richly specific performance as Mi-ok peels back the layers of agency involved in sharing one's story at all. Unlike her husband, Mi-ok is more than eager to have cameras follow them around and be interviewed about the layoffs, even though she herself never worked at the auto plant. It's a credit to Jeon that Mi-ok doesn't come off as a craven opportunist; instead she represents decades' worth of cultural shifts that have primed most of us to maintain a "public presence" (social media or otherwise) or view everyone as the star of their own self-aware Truman Show. She also clearly hopes that participating in the documentary might help open Ho-seuk up into finally confronting his trauma.

Throughout the film, an unspoken push and pull for narrative control is both subtext and text. At one point, Mi-ok bluntly asks Ye-ji the value of the shirt she's wearing, in order to make plain the obvious: "I think your clothing stands out here. You are interviewing workers who are struggling, Ye-ji. I don't know, I just think it stands out a bit, and it's probably not helping." Ye-ji deflects with a nervous, embarrassed laugh, and a knowing smirk slides across Mi-ok's face; in that moment, at least, the subject turns the attention to the creator and exerts the soft power of sensible authority.

It's difficult to view all of this and not think of two other recent films: last year's No Other Choice , another searing Korean film about the indignities of corporate restructuring, and more recently You Can See Everything , the Elizabeth Holmes documentary that unfolds as a prickly tug-of-war for control over the disgraced businesswoman's image. Possible Love 's execution is more subdued than either of those projects, but no less explosive in its intensity, rage, and excavation of a certain kind of emotional truth. In the film's third act, Ye-ji and Sang-woo invite Mi-ok, Ho-seuk, and their young son to their palatial beachside estate, where the divide between performance and reality and the haves and have nots must finally be reckoned with. When the tension is ultimately released, the resolution is both surprising yet mundane; it feels exactly right.

This piece also appears in NPR's Pop Culture Happy Hour newsletter. Sign up for the newsletter so you don't miss the next one, plus get weekly recommendations about what's making us happy.

Listen to Pop Culture Happy Hour on Apple Podcasts and Spotify .

item.title: Hegseth's failed impeachment was a warning to Democrats. Where will they go from here?
item.description: Democrats are not in the majority yet , but the first post-election test of their ability to get things done was a failure. The House was unable to advance an impeachment effort of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Eleven Democrats were no-shows for the vote. Based on the math in this vote: If those 11 had been there and if no more Republicans showed up, the attempt would have gone forward.
item.content:encoded:
Democrats are not in the majority yet , but the first post-election test of their ability to get things done was a failure.

The House was unable to advance an impeachment effort of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Eleven Democrats were no-shows for the vote. Based on the math in this vote: If those 11 had been there and if no more Republicans showed up, the attempt would have gone forward.

Now, for those who want to see Hegseth impeached, it's fair to ask why only one Republican was in favor of it, Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, who led the effort , especially after an election that saw GOP wipeouts in no small measure because of the Iran war? The GOP still controls the floor, so a Democratic speaker would have been able to leave the vote open longer for the 11 to be able to cast their votes.

But it's also fair to ask if this would have happened under Nancy Pelosi's watch? (Ironically, she was one of the 11 who didn't vote for advancing Hegseth's impeachment because she had flown back to San Francisco for a veterans' event.) Or if this kind of effort is what people want in the first place.

First, on the Pelosi point: The former House speaker and retiring congresswoman was known for the discipline she kept in her caucus. She knew where the votes were, who was voting how and why – and, most importantly, did not move forward with efforts that didn't have the votes.

Hakeem Jeffries, the heir apparent Democratic leader , is going to have the largest majority in Congress since the early 1990s. His leadership and agenda priorities are going to be scrutinized and compared to Pelosi – and this wasn't a great start to this new era.

Second, on whether impeachments are what people want to see: it depends on which people. Certainly, the Democratic base — and some beyond that — wants accountability for the Trump administration.

Voters more broadly also said corruption was a top issue in the campaign. But walking the line between reasonable accountability and oversight versus impeachments is a potential tight rope.

Democrats will have to balance the mandate they were given to bring down prices (sound familiar?) and end the war with the accountability of the Trump administration that many in the Democratic base feverishly wants and expects.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll taken after the election, found that 8-in-10 people think Democrats' focus in the first 100 days should be on the cost of living, three-quarters said lowering health care costs, 7 in 10 said lowering gas prices, while 6 in 10 said ending the Iran war and eliminating President Trump's tariffs.

What about investigations and impeachment? Only 40% said investigating the Trump administration should be a priority in those early days. But 71% of Democrats do want this to be a first 100 days focus. Only 36% of independents said the same.

Almost two-thirds said they are concerned that Democrats will spend too much time on investigations, which included, by the way, half of Democrats.

When it comes specifically to pursuing impeachment of Trump, only 33% said they think it would be good for the country. On the other hand, 63% of Democrats do. Only 30% of independents said it would be good for the country.

More than half also said they think Democrats should at least make efforts to work with the Trump administration. That, however, only included 40% of Democrats.

So this is going to be tricky to navigate for Democratic leadership, but a major part of a speaker's job is messaging, particularly when that speaker's party does not control the White House.

People are going to be watching the new Democratic majority for what it focuses on, and even with the Hegseth effort, it was clear that many conservatives were thrilled with not only how it went but that Democrats were fueling Massie's effort.

It arguably backfired and strengthened Hegseth's position within the administration. The White House and Republicans rallied around him. Even if some Republicans on Capitol Hill might have misgivings with Hegseth for one reason or another, and they and Vice President Vance think the war in Iran was the main reason for the midterm losses, opposing Democrats is far more unifying.

Politics is often (some would say too often) a team sport, and no group is more conditioned to put the T-shirt on and run the playbook than the red team.

It certainly gave Republicans more of a chance to go on offense than talking about health care, the cost of living or the war and gas prices.

Democratic leadership is certainly aware of the line it has to walk, but Jeffries is going to have to make some decisions. Asked on PBS NewsHour this week if Democrats would be impeaching more Trump officials, he said, "We will cross that bridge when we get to it."

But a House speaker is the one who builds the legislative bridges. He or she controls the agenda.

Jeffries, of course, also noted, as he has elsewhere, that affordability is a priority.

"We're committed to driving down the high cost of living in every area," he said. "That's housing, that's health care, that's groceries, that's gas, that's caregiving – to making this country affordable again for everyone."

Democrats have been given a huge opportunity with majorities in both the House and Senate — but the balance of priorities, timing, messaging and discipline are all going to be major tests.

The stakes couldn't be higher. Arguably, what Democrats focus on will lay the foundation for views of the party's competence heading into the 2028 presidential election, and they don't want to squander the advantages they have.

The Ipsos poll showed that Democrats have big leads on which party has a better plan, policy or approach for health care (42%-23%), the cost of living (40%-25%) and the economy (37%-30%).

But they have to be careful. A lot of people are not convinced that Democrats are focused on the issues that are important to them. Only 47% in the Ipsos poll said that, including only 40% of independents.

Only 44% said they're confident that Democrats are putting the best interests of the American people above their own personal interests.

So while Democrats have the wind at their backs, the jury is still out on whether people are confident in their leadership.
